concepts.def: Heart, blood and vessels transporting substances around the body (double circulation).
Oxygen in and carbon dioxide out across large, thin, moist surfaces.
Loss of water vapour from leaves, pulling water up the xylem.
Xylem carries water and minerals up; phloem carries sugars (translocation).
Breathing moves air; respiration releases energy inside cells.
Removal of metabolic waste such as carbon dioxide and urea.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Structures & Functions in Living Organisms — a core area of GCSE Biology.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Structures & Functions in Living Organisms brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Structures & Functions in Living Organisms.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: Which of these is a prokaryote?
options: Human skin cell
Yeast
Bacterium
Onion cell
protein synthesis
photosynthesis
aerobic respiration
cell division

mcqs.q: How does a population of organisms become better adapted to its environment over time?
options: Individuals with advantageous heritable variations survive and reproduce more; their alleles increase in frequency over generations.
Vaccines insert new genes into your DNA permanently.
Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
Individual organisms change during their lifetime in response to their environment and pass the changes on to offspring.

mcqs.q: During an action potential, do Na+ and K+ move through the same channels?
options: Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.
Na+ and K+ swap places through the same channel at the same time.
Organisms decide what features they need and grow them by force of will.
No — voltage-gated Na+ channels open first (depolarisation, Na+ in), then voltage-gated K+ channels open (repolarisation, K+ out).

mcqs.q: What is actually transferred to the body when you get a vaccine?
options: Antigens (often from weakened, dead, or fragmented pathogens) that train the immune system to make memory cells.
Vaccines insert new genes into your DNA permanently.
Vaccines inject ready-made antibodies directly into the bloodstream.
Only Na+ moves during an action potential; K+ stays still.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Specialised cells”?
options: The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Stem cell”?
options: Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Subcellular structures”?
options: Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
Cells adapted for a specific role, e.g. red blood cell, sperm, root hair.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Eukaryotic cell”?
options: A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Cell”?
options: A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
Parts inside a cell with specific jobs: nucleus, mitochondria, ribosomes, chloroplasts.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.

mcqs.q: Which of these is the best definition of “Prokaryotic cell”?
options: A cell with a nucleus enclosed in a membrane; e.g. animal, plant, fungus cells.
Undifferentiated cell that can divide to form many cell types.
A smaller cell with no nucleus; DNA is a loop in the cytoplasm; e.g. bacteria.
The smallest unit of life; carries out the functions needed to live.

mcqs.q: A bacterium is 2 µm long. How many fit end-to-end across a 1 mm gap?
options: 500 bacteria
750 bacteria
400 bacteria
250 bacteria

mcqs.q: A root hair cell has a long, thin extension. How does this adapt it for taking up water and minerals?
options: It increases the surface area for absorption.
It stores starch for the plant.
It allows photosynthesis in the root.
It pumps water using a heart-like action.

mcqs.q: Which sequence correctly shows levels of organisation in a flowering plant?
options: Cell → tissue → organ → organ system
Organ → tissue → cell
Tissue → organ → cell
Organ system → cell → tissue

mcqs.q: The small intestine is adapted for absorption by having villi. The main benefit of villi is to:
options: Increase the surface area for absorbing digested food
Produce bile to emulsify fats
Slow food down so it is not absorbed
Carry out respiration for the gut

mcqs.q: Which structure in a leaf controls gas exchange and water loss?
options: The stomata
The xylem
The waxy cuticle
The root hairs

sequence.def: Smallest unit of life; basic building block of all organisms
Group of similar cells working together, e.g. muscle tissue
Several tissues combined for a function, e.g. the heart
Group of organs working together, e.g. circulatory system
Complete living individual built from all organ systems
